title: 6 ways large loads are reshaping power market policy
gist: Wood Mackenzie lists six policy trends reshaping power markets as data-centre-led large loads strain grids built for flat demand: interruptible service, large-load tariffs, efficiency standards, readiness-based interconnection, siting rules and co-located generation treatment. The common aim is to balance speed to power, reliability and affordability.

insights.claim: Interruptible service options, voluntary or compulsory, are becoming commonplace in speed-to-power proposals, letting utilities serve large loads even when reliability cannot be fully guaranteed.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Data centres may trade firm service for faster connection, shaping the value of onsite backup and flexible load.
insights.quote: Flexible service options are becoming commonplace in speed-to-power proposals.
insights.locator: 1. Interruptible service options and queue prioritisation

insights.claim: Large load tariffs and cost allocation methodologies aim to make large customers pay the true cost of serving them, isolating grid upgrade costs so existing customers are shielded.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Higher data centre power costs and lower political risk for utilities' rate cases; large-load customers have legitimate objections.
insights.locator: 2. Large load tariffs and cost allocation methodologies

insights.claim: PG&E aims to use large-load growth to support the grid and improve overall affordability for its customers.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Utilities see large loads as a way to spread fixed costs, which could support rate base growth narratives.

insights.claim: AI is driving a surge in speculative data centre projects, so regulators are adopting readiness-based interconnection criteria to ensure only financially committed, shovel-ready projects use grid operator resources.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Expect queue attrition and a pipeline that overstates real demand; committed developers gain priority.

insights.claim: Jurisdictional differences and a fast-changing political climate let large-load customers shop around for the best regulatory conditions and hedge their bets.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Regulatory arbitrage will shift data centre location decisions between states and countries.
insights.quote: shop around for the best regulatory conditions and ‘hedge their bets’

insights.claim: Regulators are using zoning to align data centre development with national economic and digital sovereignty goals, with strategic growth zones a key focus in Asia, and permitting is consolidating across jurisdictions.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Sovereignty-driven siting favours designated zones and domestic capacity over free-market placement.

insights.claim: Efficiency compliance standards for data centres are increasingly a prerequisite for interconnection or zoning approval, particularly in Europe.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Efficiency mandates can raise compliance cost and favour efficient cooling and power equipment.

insights.claim: Siting data centres at or near generation plants has become a popular route to faster interconnection, alongside onsite generation, distributed resources and virtual power plants, with reforms emerging on how behind-the-meter generation interacts with the grid.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Supports demand for onsite gas, storage and distributed resources, and independent power producers with sites.

insights.claim: Surging data-centre-led electricity demand is challenging grid operators and utilities used to decades of flat demand, forcing rewrites of planning and cost allocation rules.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Regulatory regimes, not just supply, will determine who captures data centre power spend.
insights.quote: Unprecedented large-load development is forcing stakeholders to rewrite the rules
